A  How ions form

IGCSE Edexcel Chemistry · Topic booklet
1.37 · ions formed by electron loss or gain
Name:
Key ideas
  • An ion is a charged particle made when an atom loses or gains electrons.
  • Metals lose their outer electrons → positive ions (cations).
  • Non-metals gain electrons → negative ions (anions).
  • Both end up with a full outer shell, the same electron arrangement as a noble gas.
  • The number of protons does not change. Charge = protons − electrons.

D  Giant ionic lattices

IGCSE Edexcel Chemistry · Topic booklet
1.41–1.43 · electrostatic attraction, melting points, conductivity
Name:
Key ideas
  • Ionic bonding = strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
  • The ions form a giant lattice: a regular 3D arrangement, with attractions acting in all directions.
  • High melting and boiling points: a lot of energy is needed to overcome the many strong attractions.
  • Bigger charges (e.g. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻) → stronger attraction → higher melting point.
  • Conductivity: solid ✗ (ions fixed in place) · molten ✓ · dissolved in water ✓ (ions free to move and carry charge).
Sodium chloride lattice: small Na⁺ (+), large Cl⁻ (−)

E  Covalent bonds

IGCSE Edexcel Chemistry · Topic booklet
1.44–1.45 · shared pairs of electrons, electrostatic attraction
Name:
Key ideas
  • A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms (usually non-metals).
  • Each atom shares electrons until it has a full outer shell.
  • The bond is the electrostatic attraction between the shared pair (negative) and the nuclei (positive) of both atoms.
  • 1 shared pair = single bond, 2 = double bond, 3 = triple bond. Pairs that are not shared are lone pairs.
Both nuclei attract the shared pair: this holds the atoms together

G  Simple molecular substances

IGCSE Edexcel Chemistry · Topic booklet
1.47–1.48 · intermolecular forces, melting points and relative molecular mass
Name:
Key ideas
  • Simple molecular substances are made of small molecules. Inside each molecule: strong covalent bonds. Between molecules: weak intermolecular forces.
  • Melting or boiling only overcomes the intermolecular forces. The covalent bonds do not break.
  • Little energy is needed → low melting and boiling points (often gases or liquids at room temperature).
  • Bigger molecules (higher relative molecular mass, Mr) → stronger intermolecular forces → higher boiling point.
  • No ions and no free electrons → they don't conduct electricity.

H  Giant covalent structures

IGCSE Edexcel Chemistry · Topic booklet
1.49–1.51 · diamond, graphite and C₆₀ fullerene

Key ideas
  • Giant covalent substances: every atom is joined to others by strong covalent bonds in a huge network. Melting means breaking many strong covalent bonds → very high melting points.
  • Covalent substances don't usually conduct (no ions, no free electrons). Graphite is the exception.

Graphite: layers of hexagons, each C bonded to 3; weak forces between layers (dashed)

  • Award one mark per point unless the question says otherwise. Accept any wording that gives the same chemistry.

  • The three most common lost marks in this topic:
    • saying covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance melts or boils;
    • saying electrons carry the current in molten or dissolved ionic compounds (it is the ions);
    • missing brackets in formulae with more than one compound ion.
  • Dot-and-cross diagrams: dots and crosses may be swapped, inner shells are not needed, and circles do not have to overlap neatly as long as the shared pairs are clearly between the two atoms.
  • After marking, go back to the Check your progress table on page 12 of the booklet and shade your confidence for each line.

  • The three most common lost marks in this topic:
    • saying covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance melts or boils;
    • saying electrons carry the current in molten or dissolved ionic compounds (it is the ions);
    • missing brackets in formulae with more than one compound ion.
  • Dot-and-cross diagrams: dots and crosses may be swapped, inner shells are not needed, and circles do not have to overlap neatly as long as the shared pairs are clearly between the two atoms.
  • After marking, go back to the Check your progress table on page 12 of the booklet and shade your confidence for each line.

F  Forces, vectors and scalars

IGCSE Edexcel Physics · Topic booklet
1.11–1.14 · effects of forces, types of force, vectors and scalars, force is a vector
Name:
Key ideas
  • A force can change an object’s speed, its direction of motion, or its shape.
  • Forces act between two objects. Measured in newtons (N).
  • Non-contact forces act at a distance: gravitational (weight), electrostatic, magnetic.
  • Contact forces: friction, air resistance (drag), tension, normal reaction, upthrust.
  • A scalar has size (magnitude) only, e.g. speed, distance, mass, time, energy.
  • A vector has size and direction, e.g. velocity, displacement, force, weight, acceleration.
  • Force is a vector, so we draw it as an arrow: length = size, arrowhead = direction.

Name:
Key ideas
  • The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together.
  • Forces in the same direction add; forces in opposite directions subtract. Give the size and the direction.
  • Resultant = 0 → forces are balanced: a stationary object stays still; a moving object keeps the same velocity.
  • Resultant ≠ 0 → the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant (speeds up, slows down or changes direction).
  • Friction always acts in the opposite direction to the motion. Air resistance (drag) is friction from the air and gets bigger as speed increases.

  • On Earth g = 10 N/kg.

  • Braking distance: distance travelled while the brakes are on.

J  Falling objects and terminal velocity

IGCSE Edexcel Physics · Topic booklet
1.21 · forces on falling objects; why they reach a terminal velocity
Name:
Key ideas
  • A falling object has two forces on it: weight (down, stays the same) and air resistance (up, increases as speed increases).
  • At first only weight acts, so it accelerates at 10 m/s². As it speeds up, air resistance grows, the resultant force gets smaller, so the acceleration decreases.
  • When air resistance = weight, the resultant force is zero, so the velocity stays constant: this is terminal velocity.
  • Opening a parachute increases the surface area, so air resistance becomes bigger than weight: the resultant is upwards and the skydiver slows down until the forces balance again at a lower terminal velocity.

IGCSE Edexcel Physics · Topic booklet
1.22–1.24 · extension against force for springs, wires and rubber bands; Hooke’s law; elastic behaviour
Name:
Key ideas
  • extension = stretched length − original length
  • Hooke’s law: extension is directly proportional to force. The graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • This is only true for the initial linear region, up to the limit of proportionality. After that the line curves.
  • Elastic behaviour: the material returns to its original shape when the force is removed.
  • Stretched too far, it is permanently deformed (stays longer).
  • Springs and metal wires obey Hooke’s law at first; rubber bands do not (their graph is curved).

J  Falling objects and terminal velocity

IGCSE Edexcel Physics · Topic booklet
1.21 · forces on falling objects; why they reach a terminal velocity
Name:
Key ideas
  • A falling object has two forces on it: weight (down, stays the same) and air resistance (up, increases as speed increases).
  • At first only weight acts, so it accelerates at 10 m/s². As it speeds up, air resistance grows, the resultant force gets smaller, so the acceleration decreases.
  • When air resistance = weight, the resultant force is zero, so the velocity stays constant: this is terminal velocity.
  • Opening a parachute increases the surface area, so air resistance becomes bigger than weight: the resultant is upwards and the skydiver slows down until the forces balance again at a lower terminal velocity.

1b · Classifying Organisms

IGCSE Edexcel Biology · KS4
1.1–1.4 · classifying unfamiliar organisms, saprotrophic nutrition, scale conversions, pathogens and viruses
Name:
Eukaryotes (nucleus): plants (multicellular, cellulose walls, chloroplasts, starch), animals (multicellular, no walls, glycogen), fungi (chitin walls, hyphae or single-celled yeast, saprotrophic, glycogen), protoctists (mostly single-celled). Prokaryotes: bacteria (no nucleus, circular chromosome + plasmids). Viruses: non-living particles (protein coat + DNA/RNA, reproduce only inside host cells).

A  Classify the mystery organisms plant, animal, fungus, protoctist, bacterium or virus (A is done for you)

Organism A
Lives in pond water. Made of one cell containing a nucleus and chloroplasts.
Organism B
Grows on damp bread as a network of thin threads with chitin cell walls. Releases enzymes onto the bread, then absorbs the products.
Organism C
A microscopic single cell with no nucleus. Its DNA is one circular loop plus smaller rings.
Organism D
Multicellular with no cell walls. Feeds on other organisms and stores carbohydrate as glycogen.
Organism E
Multicellular with cellulose cell walls. Photosynthesises and stores carbohydrate as starch.
Organism F
Smaller than any bacterium. Made of a protein coat around RNA. Copies itself only inside a living host cell.

Aprotoctistsingle cell with a nucleus and chloroplasts
B
C

A  Classify the mystery organisms

groupkey evidence from the card
Aprotoctistsingle cell with a nucleus (and chloroplasts; plants are multicellular and bacteria have no nucleus)
Bfungushyphae (threads), chitin cell walls, saprotrophic nutrition (releases enzymes, absorbs products)
Cbacteriumsingle cell with no nucleus; circular chromosome and plasmids
Danimalmulticellular, no cell walls, stores glycogen
Eplantmulticellular, cellulose cell walls, photosynthesises, stores starch

Watch out for A: students often say "plant" because it has chloroplasts, but plants are multicellular — a single cell with a nucleus and chloroplasts (like Chlorella) is a protoctist.

B  Borderline organisms: Euglena and yeast

B1. Group
protoctist
B2. Why not a plant or an animal?
Not a plant: single-celled (plants are multicellular) / swims with a flagellum / takes in food in the dark.
Not an animal: single-celled (animals are multicellular) / has chloroplasts and photosynthesises.
has both plant-like and animal-like features, and is single-celled
B3. Yeast vs bacteria and Mucor
Eukaryote (not a bacterium): yeast has a nucleus (and mitochondria / membrane-bound organelles), whereas bacteria have no nucleus.
Shares with Mucor (fungi): chitin cell wall, stores carbohydrate as glycogen, saprotrophic nutrition (no chloroplasts).
nucleus (eukaryote) · chitin wall / glycogen / no chloroplasts (fungus)
Don't confuse single-celled with prokaryotic: yeast and protoctists are single-celled eukaryotes.

C  How fungi feed: saprotrophic nutrition

C1. Order of steps
1. Hyphae grow over and into the bread.
2. Hyphae secrete digestive enzymes onto the bread.
3. Enzymes break large insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones outside the fungus.
4. Small, soluble molecules are absorbed into the hyphae.
numbers down the table: 4, 1, 3, 2
C2. Why extracellular digestion?
Enzymes are secreted outside the cells onto the food, where large molecules are broken down into small soluble ones before being absorbed.
digestion happens outside the cells, before absorption
Extra- means outside (compare extranuclear, extraterrestrial).

D  Scale and microscopes

D1. Conversion and order
0.5 mm × 1000 = 500 μm
500 μm  ·  virus, bacterium, yeast cell, Amoeba
D2. How many times longer?
5 μm ÷ 0.1 μm = 50
50 times
Convert to the same unit before comparing or dividing (1 mm = 1000 μm).
D3. Light microscope limit
The virus (0.1 μm) is smaller than the 0.2 μm limit of a light microscope, so it cannot be resolved (an electron microscope is needed).
the virus (0.1 μm < 0.2 μm)

E  Pathogens and viruses

E1. Tobacco mosaic virus
Fewer chloroplasts → less light absorbed → less photosynthesis → less glucose made → less glucose for respiration and making new cells/biomass, so slower growth.
fewer chloroplasts → less photosynthesis → less glucose → less growth
E2. Is a virus alive?
Disagree: viruses can only reproduce inside living host cells (using the host's machinery), not on their own. They have no cells and do not carry out the other life processes (nutrition, respiration, excretion, growth, sensitivity/response).
no — not cellular, cannot carry out MRS C GREN independently
State both why the student's point is limited (only inside host cells) and which other life processes are missing.
E3. Named pathogens from the spec
bacterium: Pneumococcus (causes pneumonia)  ·  protoctist: Plasmodium (causes malaria)  ·  virus: influenza virus / HIV / tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)

A2. Stages
1: the substrate collides with the active site, which has a complementary shape. 2: the substrate fits into the active site (enzyme–substrate complex) and reacts. 3: the products leave; the enzyme is unchanged.
A3. Specific
The active site has a particular shape; only a substrate with the matching (complementary) shape fits into it.
A4. Used again
The enzyme is not changed by the reaction; its active site is free for another substrate molecule.

A substance made by living things that speeds up a reaction without being used up.

partadaptation

C1
light intensity
Increasing light increases the rate, so light is limiting.
C2
At Y, light is no longer limiting — something else (CO₂) is. Raising CO₂ from 0.04% to 0.4% increases the maximum rate, proving CO₂ was the limiting factor at Y.
C3
10→32 °C: particles/enzymes have more kinetic energy, so more frequent successful collisions. Above 35 °C: enzymes denature (active site changes shape, substrate no longer fits), so rate drops to zero.

A & B  Balanced diet and energy needs

componentsource (examples)function
proteinmeat, fish, eggs, beansgrowth and repair of cells/tissues
lipidbutter, oils, nutsenergy store, thermal insulation, cell membranes
vitamin Acarrots, liver, green vegvision in dim light (prevents night blindness)
vitamin Ccitrus fruit, pepperskeeps skin/gums healthy, helps wounds heal (prevents scurvy)
vitamin Doily fish, eggs, sunlighthelps absorb calcium for bones/teeth (prevents rickets)
calcium ionsmilk, cheese, yoghurtstrong bones and teeth
iron ionsred meat, spinach, beansmakes haemoglobin in red blood cells to carry O₂ (prevents anaemia)
waterdrinks, fruit, vegsolvent for chemical reactions, transport in blood, cooling
dietary fibrewholemeal bread, oats, vegadds bulk so gut muscles can push food along (prevents constipation)
B1
More physical activity (muscles contract more) AND still growing, so needs more energy from respiration.
B2
(a) Pregnancy: extra energy needed for the growing fetus and carrying extra mass. (b) Old age: generally less active and no longer growing, so lower energy need.
Key terms: malnutrition (too much or too little of a nutrient), roughage (dietary fibre for peristalsis), metabolic rate (rate of chemical reactions). Deficiency diseases: vitamin C → scurvy, vitamin D/calcium → rickets, iron → anaemia.

C & D  Alimentary canal and peristalsis

organfunction
Amouthchews food (mechanical digestion); saliva contains amylase to digest starch
Boesophagusmuscular tube pushing food to the stomach by peristalsis
Cliverproduces bile
Dgall bladderstores bile before releasing it into the duodenum
Estomachchurns food; hydrochloric acid kills bacteria & gives low pH for protease
Fpancreassecretes digestive enzymes (amylase, protease, lipase) into the duodenum
Gduodenumfirst part of small intestine; receives bile and pancreatic juice to complete digestion
Hileumsecond part of small intestine; absorbs digested food molecules into blood/lacteals
Icolon (large intestine)absorbs excess water back into the blood
Jrectumstores faeces before egestion through the anus
D1
Circular muscles behind the bolus contract (squeezing the gut narrower) while muscles in front relax, pushing the bolus forward in waves.
D2
Fibre is not digested, giving gut muscles solid bulk to grip and push against. Peristalsis uses muscular waves, not gravity, so astronauts can still swallow in space.
Don’t confuse egestion (removing undigested faeces) with excretion (removing metabolic waste made inside cells). Peristalsis uses circular and longitudinal muscles; ingestion = taking food in; assimilation = cells using absorbed food.

E & F  Enzymes and bile

enzymesubstrateproduct(s)where it acts
amylasestarchmaltosemouth, small intestine (duodenum)
maltasemaltoseglucosesmall intestine
proteaseproteinamino acidsstomach, small intestine
lipaselipid (fats/oils)fatty acids + glycerolsmall intestine
E2
Large molecules are insoluble and too big to pass through the gut wall; digestion breaks them into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.
E3
1. Kills bacteria in food. 2. Provides the low (acidic) optimum pH for stomach protease (pepsin).
F1–F2
F1: liver · gall bladder · duodenum (small intestine). F2: emulsification.
F3
1. Bile is alkaline, so it neutralises stomach acid to give the optimum pH for lipase/small-intestine enzymes. 2. It emulsifies large lipid drops into tiny droplets, giving a much larger surface area for lipase to work faster.
F4
Bile is NOT an enzyme and does NOT break lipid molecules into fatty acids and glycerol. It physically emulsifies lipids into tiny droplets; lipase is the enzyme that digests them.
Examiners love catching students calling bile an enzyme — never do!

G & H  Absorption and coeliac disease

G1–G3
P: epithelium (one cell thick). Q: blood capillary (absorbs glucose & amino acids). R: lacteal (absorbs fatty acids & glycerol).
G4
Long/villi/microvilli → huge surface area · 1-cell-thick epithelium → short diffusion distance · rich capillaries → carry molecules away to keep a steep concentration gradient · lacteal → transports absorbed lipids.
H1
Flattened villi give a much smaller surface area in the small intestine → far less glucose and amino acids absorbed into the blood → less glucose reaches cells for respiration (feeling tired) and less nutrient absorption for growth/storage (weight loss).
Link structural change (flattened villi) → smaller surface area → less absorption → less glucose for respiration.
Villus adaptations (4 key ideas): microvilli (huge surface area), wall one cell thick (short diffusion distance), dense capillary network (maintains steep gradient), and lacteal (absorbs fatty acids and glycerol).

Oestrogen rises in the first half of the cycle and makes the uterus lining thicken / repair after the period. Progesterone rises after ovulation and keeps the lining thick. When progesterone falls, the lining breaks down (menstruation).
Don't say progesterone builds the lining: that's oestrogen.
Key terms: ovulation = egg release (~day 14); menstruation = shedding the uterus lining. High progesterone inhibits further ovulation and maintains the lining during pregnancy.

C  Fertilisation to embryo

C1
The nucleus of the sperm fuses with the nucleus of the egg (fertilisation), making a zygote. The zygote divides by mitosis many times into a ball of cells, the embryo, which implants in the uterus lining.
"The sperm enters the egg" alone is not enough: the nuclei fuse.

D  The placenta and amniotic fluid

D1
oxygen, glucose and amino acids: mother → embryo · carbon dioxide, urea: embryo → mother
D2
By diffusion between the two blood supplies, which are very close together in the placenta.
D3
The embryo floats in it; the fluid cushions it against bumps (a shock absorber).
The mother’s and baby’s blood do not mix in the placenta — substances cross by diffusion across thin walls. The umbilical cord carries blood between foetus and placenta; the amnion holds the amniotic fluid.

E  Puberty

E1
voice deepens: testosterone · hips widen: oestrogen · breasts develop: oestrogen · facial hair grows: testosterone · pubic and underarm hair grows: both · muscles develop more: testosterone · periods start: oestrogen
E2
It is a primary sexual characteristic: part of the job of the reproductive organs themselves.

D1the Sun (light energy, trapped by photosynthesis)
D2the direction energy (and food) is transferred: from the food to the feeder
D3oak tree and grass
D4caterpillar, aphid, rabbit
D5caterpillar, aphid or rabbit
D6blue tit, ladybird, fox or sparrowhawk

D8blue tit

D13

Food-web arrows always point in the direction of energy transfer (from eaten → eater), never "who eats whom". Predators feeding on prey is predation (a biotic factor).

E  Pyramids

E2
One oak tree is huge and feeds thousands of caterpillars, so the bottom bar is narrower than the one above.
E3
Energy is lost at every level (respiration, heat, waste), so each level always has less energy than the one below.

F1
2400 ÷ 24 000 × 100 = 10; 200 ÷ 2400 × 100 = 8.3
grass → rabbits 10% · rabbits → foxes 8.3%
F2
Any three: respiration (heat), movement, not all of the rabbit is eaten (bones, fur), egestion (faeces), excretion (urine).
F3
About 90% of the energy is lost at each level, so after a few levels there is too little energy left to support another population.

G  Moving substances

G1
Carbon compounds in the grass are eaten and digested by the rabbit and become part of its body; the fox eats the rabbit. Respiration in all of them (and decomposers breaking down dead bodies and waste) releases carbon dioxide into the air.

IGCSE Edexcel Chemistry · KS4
1.25–1.26 · spec sub-topic 1(e) part 1: word equations, balanced equations with state symbols, relative formula mass
Name:
Reminder: balancing
Atoms are not made or destroyed in a reaction, so there must be the same number of each atom on both sides. Balance by writing big numbers in front of formulae. Never change the small numbers — that would make a different substance. A big number multiplies everything in the formula after it, including anything in brackets: 2Ca(OH)2 has 2 Ca, 4 O and 4 H.
Worked example: hydrogen + oxygen → water
H2 + O2 → H2O   O: 2 on the left, 1 on the right ✗
H2 + O2 → 2H2O   O fixed, but now H: 2 left, 4 right ✗
2H2 + O2 → 2H2O   H 4 = 4, O 2 = 2 ✓
atomleftright
H2 × 2 = 42 × 2 = 4
O22 × 1 = 2

Reminder: three steps

Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it reacts/corrodes in place of the steel pipe. Copper is less reactive than iron, so iron would corrode even faster instead.

F1
In the table order: 3, 6, 1, 5, 2, 4
Warm acid → add oxide to excess → filter → evaporate until crystals start → cool → filter and dry.

So all the acid reacts (no acid left in the salt). You can see black solid left that won't dissolve.

The crystals are hydrated: they need water of crystallisation. Heating to dryness would give white powder (anhydrous) or spit.

Black solid + colourless acid → blue solution (blue crystals).
Crystallisation wording: evaporate gently to reach the point of crystallisation (a hot saturated solution) so water of crystallisation stays in the crystals — heating to dryness makes anhydrous powder.

Use hydrochloric acid. Add zinc carbonate to warm acid until fizzing stops and some solid is left (excess). Filter off the excess. sheets.title: Cells and Atoms: Understanding the Basics
sheets.oldHtml:
Cells and Atoms: Understanding the Basics

Common Misconceptions Worksheet
Common Misconception: Many students think that things are made EITHER of cells OR of atoms - that these are two completely different categories.

The Truth: Cells are MADE OF atoms! Everything is made of atoms. Living things organize atoms into molecules, and molecules into cells. Non-living things are made of atoms and molecules but NOT organized into cells.

Section A: Understanding the Hierarchy

1. Complete the following sentence: [1]

Atoms join together to form _______________, which can then be organized into _______________ in living organisms.

2. True or False: A cell is made of atoms. [1]
3. Sarah says: "My textbook is made of atoms, but my skin is made of cells. They're completely different things." [3]

Explain what is wrong with Sarah's statement.

Section B: Cells vs Atoms in Real Examples

4. Consider a slice of bread. The bread was made from wheat, which is a living plant. [4]

a) Is bread made of atoms? Explain your answer.

b) Does bread contain cells? Explain your answer.

c) Are the atoms and cells in bread the same thing, or are they different? Explain.

5. Complete the table below by putting a tick (✓) in the appropriate boxes. [6]
Example Made of atoms? Made of cells?
A rock
A human being
A water molecule (H₂O)
A bacterial cell
A wooden chair
A cotton T-shirt

Section C: Thinking Deeper

6. A student examines a leaf under a microscope and can see individual plant cells. [2]

If they could zoom in even further (beyond what a normal microscope can do), what would they see that makes up those cells?

7. Put the following in order from SMALLEST to LARGEST: [2]

Cell, Atom, Organ, Molecule, Organism

8. Explain why it is correct to say that a living organism is made of BOTH cells AND atoms. [3]

Section D: Application Questions

9. Two students are discussing a piece of cheese. [4]

Student A: "Cheese is made from milk, which comes from cows. Cows are alive, so cheese must be made of cells."

Student B: "But cheese isn't alive anymore, so it's just made of atoms and molecules now, not cells."

a) Which student is more correct? Explain your reasoning.

b) What would both students need to understand about the relationship between cells and atoms?

10. Draw a simple diagram showing how atoms, molecules, and cells are related in a living organism. Label your diagram clearly. [4]
Draw your diagram here
11. A scientist discovers a new object on another planet. They need to determine if it is living or non-living. [5]

a) Will the object definitely be made of atoms, whether it's living or non-living?

b) If the object is made of cells, what can the scientist conclude?

c) If the object is NOT made of cells, does that mean it's not made of atoms? Explain.

Section E: Challenge Questions

12. Consider a DNA molecule inside a human cell. [3]

Explain the relationship between the atoms, the DNA molecule, and the cell. Which contains which?

13. A piece of fruit starts to decay and break down. [4]

a) Are the plant cells in the fruit still made of atoms during the decay process?

b) As the cells break down, what happens to the atoms that made them up?

c) Why is this evidence that atoms and cells are not mutually exclusive categories?

Total: 42 marks

Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
1.1 FDP Conversions
1.2 Calculations
Key Concepts: Convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages. Calculate percentages of amounts. Percentage increase and decrease. Compound percentages. Order FDP values.

Section A: Conversions

1. Convert the following: [4]
(a) 3/5 to a decimal and percentage
(b) 0.24 to a fraction and percentage
(c) 35% to a decimal and fraction
(d) 0.625 to a percentage and simplest fraction
2. Arrange in order from smallest to largest: 3/8, 0.37, 36% [2]

Section B: Percentage Calculations

3. Calculate: [4]
(a) 15% of £240
(b) 8% of 450 kg
(c) What percentage is 18 out of 45?
(d) If 30% of a number is 27, find the number
4. A jacket costs £80. It's on sale for 25% off. [2]
(a) Calculate the sale price
(b) What was the original price if the sale price is now £60?

Section C: Compound Percentages

5. A house worth £200,000 increases in value by 5% each year. [3]
(a) Calculate the value after 1 year
(b) Calculate the value after 3 years
Total marks: 20

Mark Scheme

1. (a) 0.6, 60% [1]
(b) 6/25, 24% [1]
(c) 0.35, 7/20 [1]
(d) 62.5%, 5/8 [1]
2. 3/8 = 0.375, 36% = 0.36; So 36%, 3/8, 0.37 [2]
3. (a) 0.15 × 240 = £36 [1]
(b) 0.08 × 450 = 36 kg [1]
(c) (18/45) × 100 = 40% [1]
(d) 27 ÷ 0.30 = 90 [1]
4. (a) 80 × 0.75 = £60 [1]
(b) 60 ÷ 0.75 = £80 [1]
5. (a) 200,000 × 1.05 = £210,000 [1]
(b) 200,000 × (1.05)³ = £231,525.25 [2]

Surds and Indices

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
1.3 Surds
1.4 Indices
Key Concepts: Laws of indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, a⁰ = 1, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. Surds are irrational roots. Simplify surds by factoring out perfect squares.

Section A: Laws of Indices

1. Simplify using laws of indices: [4]
(a) 2³ × 2⁵
(b) (3²)³
(c) 5⁻²
(d) 161/2
2. Simplify: 8a6b32a2b5 [2]

Section B: Surds

3. Simplify the following surds: [4]
(a) √48
(b) √12 + √27
(c) 2√5 × 3√2
(d) √82
4. Rationalize the denominator: 3√5 [2]

Section C: Mixed Problems

5. Solve: 2(x-1) = 8 [2]
6. Simplify: (√18 × √2) + (31/2)² [2]
Total marks: 20

1. (a) 2⁸ = 256 [1]
(b) 3⁶ = 729 [1]
(c) 1/25 [1]
(d) 4 [1]
2. (8÷2) × (a6a2) × (b3b5) = 4a4b−2 = 4a4b2 [2]
3. (a) √(16×3) = 4√3 [1]
(b) 2√3 + 3√3 = 5√3 [1]
(c) 6√10 [1]
(d) 2√2÷2 = √2 [1]
4. 3√5 × √5√5 = 3√55 [2]
5. 2(x-1) = 2³; x-1 = 3; x = 4 [2]
6. √36 + 3 = 6 + 3 = 9 [2]

Prime Factors and Standard Form

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
1.4 Prime Factors
1.5 Standard Form
Key Concepts: Prime factorization uses only prime numbers. Highest common factor (HCF) is common primes with smallest powers. Lowest common multiple (LCM) uses all primes with greatest powers. Standard form is A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10.

Section A: Prime Factors

1. Write as a product of primes: [4]
(a) 84
(b) 180
(c) 315
(d) 512
2. Find the HCF and LCM of 60 and 96. [3]

Section B: Standard Form

3. Write in standard form: [3]
(a) 34,500
(b) 0.00072
(c) 5,960,000
4. Convert out of standard form: [3]
(a) 6.8 × 10³
(b) 4.2 × 10⁻⁴
(c) 9.01 × 10⁵

Section C: Applications

5. The mass of Earth is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg. Write this as a normal number. [2]
6. Express 1.8 × 10⁵ divided by 6 × 10² in standard form. [2]
Total marks: 17

Mark Scheme

1. (a) 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 [1]; (b) 2² × 3² × 5 [1]; (c) 3² × 5 × 7 [1]; (d) 2⁹ [1]
2. HCF = 2³ × 3 = 24 [1]; LCM = 2⁵ × 3 × 5 = 480 [2]
3. (a) 3.45 × 10⁴ [1]; (b) 7.2 × 10⁻⁴ [1]; (c) 5.96 × 10⁶ [1]
4. (a) 6,800 [1]; (b) 0.00042 [1]; (c) 901,000 [1]
5. 5,970,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg [2]
6. (1.8/6) × 10^(5-2) = 0.3 × 10³ = 3.0 × 10² [2]

sheets.spec: 1.6 Ratio & Proportion
sheets.oldHtml:
Ratio and Proportion

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
1.6 Ratio & Proportion
Key Concepts: Simplify ratios by dividing by the HCF. Ratios can be written as fractions. In direct proportion, y = kx. Inverse proportion, xy = k. Use unitary method to scale quantities.

Section A: Ratio Basics

1. Simplify these ratios: [3]
(a) 24 : 60
(b) 45 : 30 : 75
(c) 6 m : 250 cm
2. Divide £360 in the ratio 2 : 3. [2]

Section B: Proportion

3. y is directly proportional to x. If y = 18 when x = 6, find y when x = 15. [2]
4. t is inversely proportional to p. If t = 12 when p = 4, find p when t = 8. [2]

Section C: Scaling

5. A recipe for 12 cookies uses 300 g flour. How much flour is needed for 18 cookies? [2]
6. A map scale is 1:50,000. What distance on the map represents 7.5 km in reality? [2]
Total marks: 13

Mark Scheme

1. (a) 2 : 5 [1]; (b) 3 : 2 : 5 [1]; (c) 600 cm : 250 cm → 24 : 10 = 12 : 5 [1]
2. 2 parts = £144; 3 parts = £216 [2]
3. k = 18/6 = 3; y = 3 × 15 = 45 [2]
4. tp = 48; p = 48/8 = 6 [2]
5. Scale factor 18/12 = 1.5; Flour = 300 × 1.5 = 450 g [2]
6. 7.5 km = 750,000 cm; on map = 750,000 / 50,000 = 15 cm [2]

Inequalities and Linear Programming

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
2.6 Inequalities
2.7 Linear Programming
Key Concepts: Inequalities show relationships between quantities using symbols like <, >, ≤, ≥. They can be solved algebraically or graphically. Linear programming involves finding optimal solutions subject to constraints represented as inequalities.

Section A: Solving Inequalities

1. Solve the following inequalities: [3]
(a) 2x + 3 > 11
(b) 5 - 2x ≤ -3
(c) -3 < x + 2 < 5
2. Solve: 3(x - 2) ≥ 2(x + 1) [2]

Section B: Graphical Inequalities

3. On a coordinate grid, shade the region satisfying all three inequalities: [4]
x ≥ 0, y ≤ 4, x + y ≤ 6
4. Write down the three inequalities that define the shaded region bounded by the lines x = 0, y = 2, and y = x + 1. [3]

Section C: Linear Programming

5. A company makes chairs and tables. Each chair takes 2 hours to make and each table takes 3 hours. The profit per chair is £20 and per table is £30. There are 60 hours available. [4]
(a) Write the constraint inequality
(b) If the company makes 10 chairs and 10 tables, calculate the profit
(c) Suggest the combination that maximizes profit with the time constraint
6. Maximize P = 3x + 4y subject to: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + 2y ≤ 8, 2x + y ≤ 10. [3]
Total marks: 22

Mark Scheme

1. (a) 2x > 8, x > 4 [1]
(b) -2x ≤ -8, x ≥ 4 [1]
(c) -5 < x < 3 [1]
2. 3x - 6 ≥ 2x + 2 [1]
x ≥ 8 [1]
3. Correct region shaded - bounded by x = 0 (y-axis), y = 4 (horizontal line), and x + y = 6 (diagonal line) [4]
4. x ≥ 0 [1]
y ≥ 2 [1]
y ≤ x + 1 [1]
5. (a) 2c + 3t ≤ 60 [1]
(b) Profit = 20(10) + 30(10) = £500 [1]
(c) Make 0 chairs and 20 tables for maximum profit of £600 [2]
6. Test corner points: (0,0)→0, (0,4)→16, (2,3)→18, (4,2)→17, (5,0)→15 [2]
Maximum is P = 18 at (2,3) [1]

sheets.oldHtml:
Sequences and Series

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
3.1 Arithmetic Sequences
3.2 Geometric Sequences
3.3 Series & Summation
Key Concepts: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. In an arithmetic sequence, the difference between consecutive terms is constant (common difference d). In a geometric sequence, the ratio between consecutive terms is constant (common ratio r). A series is the sum of terms in a sequence.

Section A: Arithmetic Sequences and Series

1. The first term of an arithmetic sequence is 3 and the common difference is 5. [2]
(a) Write down the first five terms
(b) Find the 20th term
2. An arithmetic sequence has first term a = 2 and common difference d = 4. [2]
(a) Find the sum of the first 10 terms
(b) Which term equals 58?
3. The 3rd term of an arithmetic sequence is 11 and the 7th term is 27. [3]
Find the first term and common difference.

Section B: Geometric Sequences and Series

4. A geometric sequence has first term 2 and common ratio 3. [2]
(a) Write down the first four terms
(b) Find the 7th term
5. A geometric sequence has first term 100 and common ratio 0.5. [3]
(a) Find the sum of the first 5 terms
(b) Find the sum to infinity
6. The 2nd term of a geometric sequence is 6 and the 4th term is 24. [3]
Find the first term and common ratio.

Section C: Mixed Problems

Functions and Graphs

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
3.4 Functions
3.5 Graphs & Transformations
Key Concepts: A function is a relationship where each input has exactly one output. Functions can be represented as equations, tables, or graphs. Transformations of graphs involve translations, reflections, and stretches. The gradient of a line shows its steepness.

Section A: Functions and Notation

1. For the function f(x) = 3x - 5: [3]
(a) Find f(2)
(b) Find f(-1)
(c) Find f(x) = 10
2. Given g(x) = x² + 4x - 3: [2]
(a) Find g(3)
(b) Find g(0)

Section B: Graphs and Gradients

3. For the line 2x + 3y = 12: [3]
(a) Find the gradient
(b) Find the y-intercept
(c) State the x-intercept
4. A line passes through points (2, 5) and (6, 17). [3]
(a) Find the gradient
(b) Find the equation of the line

Section C: Quadratic Functions

5. For the quadratic function y = x² - 6x + 5: [4]
(a) Find the roots
(b) Find the coordinates of the vertex
(c) State the y-intercept
6. Sketch the graph of y = -(x - 3)² + 4, labeling key features. [3]
Total marks: 21

Mark Scheme

1. (a) f(2) = 3(2) - 5 = 1 [1]
(b) f(-1) = 3(-1) - 5 = -8 [1]
(c) 3x - 5 = 10, so x = 5 [1]
2. (a) g(3) = 9 + 12 - 3 = 18 [1]
(b) g(0) = 0 + 0 - 3 = -3 [1]
3. (a) Rearrange to y = -⅔x + 4, gradient = -⅔ [1]
(b) y-intercept = 4 [1]
(c) x-intercept = 6 [1]
4. (a) Gradient = (17-5)/(6-2) = 12/4 = 3 [1]
(b) y - 5 = 3(x - 2), so y = 3x - 1 [2]
5. (a) (x - 1)(x - 5) = 0, roots are 1 and 5 [2]
(b) Vertex at x = 3, y = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4; vertex is (3, -4) [1]
(c) y-intercept = 5 [1]
6. Vertex at (3, 4) [1]
Opens downward [1]
y-intercept at (0, -5), roots at (3±2, 0) = (1, 0) and (5, 0) [1]

sheets.oldHtml:
Angles, Triangles and Polygons

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics — Version 2
4.1A Angles
4.1D Triangles
4.2 Polygons
Key Concepts:
Angle: A measure of rotation between two lines that meet at a point.
Polygon: A closed 2D shape made from straight lines only (sides do NOT have to be equal length). The lines must not cross each other.
Regular Polygon: A special polygon where ALL sides are equal length AND ALL angles are equal.
Quadrilateral: Any polygon with exactly 4 sides.

Section A: Drawing Basic Angles

1 Draw the following angles in the boxes provided [3]

Instructions: Use your protractor to draw each angle accurately. Label each angle clearly.

a) An acute angle

(Any angle less than 90°)

b) An obtuse angle

(Any angle between 90° and 180°)

c) An angle of 56°

(Use your protractor!)

2 Draw these specific angles using your protractor [4]

a) 35°

b) 125°

c) 90° (right angle)

d) 160°

Section B: Drawing Combinations of Lines and Angles

3 Draw the following combinations of lines and angles [5]

a) Draw three lines that meet at a point, forming two acute angles

Hint: Start with a point, then draw three lines from it. Check that two of the angles formed are acute (less than 90°).

b) Draw four lines that meet at a point, with one right angle and two obtuse angles

Hint: Use your protractor to ensure accuracy.

c) Draw two intersecting lines forming angles of 45° and 135°

Hint: When two straight lines cross, they create two pairs of equal angles.

Section C: Types of Triangles

4 Draw these triangles based on the given descriptions [5]

Tip: Try drawing more than one example of each triangle type in the box to show different variations!

a) An equilateral triangle

All sides equal, all angles 60°

b) An isosceles triangle

Two sides equal, two angles equal

c) A right-angled triangle

One angle = 90°

d) A scalene triangle

All sides different lengths

e) A right-angled isosceles triangle

One 90° angle, two equal sides

Section D: Understanding and Drawing Polygons

What is a Polygon?
A polygon is a closed 2D shape made entirely from straight lines. The lines must connect to form a complete shape with no gaps. The lines must NOT cross each other. The sides do NOT have to be the same length (unless it's a regular polygon).
5 Which of these are polygons? Write YES or NO [5]

a) A triangle ___________

b) A circle ___________

c) A square ___________

d) A shape with one curved side and three straight sides ___________

e) A pentagon (5-sided shape) ___________

6 Draw these polygons in the boxes [6]

Remember: Polygons are closed shapes made only from straight lines. The sides don't have to be the same length. Use a ruler!

a) A triangle (3 sides)

b) A quadrilateral (4 sides)

c) A pentagon (5 sides)

d) A hexagon (6 sides)

e) A heptagon (7 sides)

f) An octagon (8 sides)

Section E: Regular Polygons

Regular Polygons:
A regular polygon has ALL sides equal in length AND ALL angles equal in size.
Examples: equilateral triangle, square, regular pentagon, regular hexagon
7 Draw these regular polygons as accurately as you can [4]

a) An equilateral triangle

(All sides equal, all angles 60°)

b) A square

(All sides equal, all angles 90°)

c) A regular pentagon

(5 equal sides, 5 equal angles)

d) A regular hexagon

(6 equal sides, 6 equal angles)

Section F: Special Quadrilaterals

8 Draw a few examples of each special quadrilateral [12]

Use a ruler and pay attention to the specific properties of each shape!

a) Squares

All sides equal, all angles 90°

b) Rectangles (not squares)

Opposite sides equal, all angles 90°

c) Rhombuses

All sides equal, opposite angles equal

d) Parallelograms (not rectangles)

Opposite sides parallel and equal

e) Kites

Two pairs of adjacent equal sides

f) Trapeziums

One pair of parallel sides

Section G: Combining Polygons and Angles

9 Draw shapes with specific angle requirements [6]

a) Draw a quadrilateral with two right angles, one acute angle and one obtuse angle

Hint: Angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Two right angles account for 180°, so the remaining two angles must also sum to 180° — meaning one must be acute and one obtuse. Label all four angles clearly.

b) Draw a pentagon where three angles are 90° and mark them

Hint: Angles in a pentagon sum to 540°. Three right angles account for 270°, leaving 270° shared between the other two angles. Try drawing a staircase-style or L-shaped pentagon. Use the right angle symbol to mark the 90° angles.

c) Draw an octagon with at least four right angles

Hint: An octagon has 8 sides. Try drawing a staircase or cross-like shape — these naturally produce right angles. Your octagon will be non-convex (some corners will point inward).

10 Create composite shapes (combining polygons) [6]

a) Draw a shape made by joining two equilateral triangles together along one side

What is this shape called?

Name: _______________________________________________

b) Draw a hexagon by combining a square and two equilateral triangles

Place one triangle on top of the square and one on the bottom.

c) Draw a pattern using at least 3 regular polygons of your choice

Be creative! The polygons can be the same or different types.

Total: 56 marks

Mark Scheme

1. [3] — 1 mark each for:
(a) Any angle clearly less than 90°, labelled as acute.
(b) Any angle clearly between 90° and 180°, labelled as obtuse.
(c) An angle of 56° ± 2°, drawn with a protractor and labelled.
2. [4] — 1 mark each for angles within ± 2°:
(a) 35°   (b) 125°   (c) 90° (right angle symbol acceptable)   (d) 160°
3. [5]
(a) [2] Three rays from a common point; two of the three gaps between rays are acute (less than 90°). The third gap will be a reflex angle. Award 1 mark for three rays meeting at a point, 1 mark for two visible acute angles.
(b) [2] Four rays from a common point; one gap is 90° (± 2°), and at least two other gaps are obtuse. Award 1 mark for correct structure, 1 mark for correct angle types.
(c) [1] Two straight lines crossing; all four angles labelled as 45°, 135°, 45°, 135° (or angles showing two pairs of equal vertically opposite angles).
4. [5] — 1 mark each for a correctly drawn and labelled example:
(a) Equilateral triangle: all three sides equal length, all angles 60°.
(b) Isosceles triangle: exactly two sides equal, base angles equal.
(c) Right-angled triangle: one angle of 90° (right angle symbol required).
(d) Scalene triangle: all three sides visibly different lengths.
(e) Right-angled isosceles triangle: one 90° angle and two 45° angles; two equal sides.
5. [5] — 1 mark each:
(a) YES   (b) NO (circle has a curved side)   (c) YES   (d) NO (has a curved side)   (e) YES
6. [6] — 1 mark each for a closed shape with straight lines only and the correct number of sides:
(a) 3 sides   (b) 4 sides   (c) 5 sides   (d) 6 sides   (e) 7 sides   (f) 8 sides.
Sides do not need to be equal. Shape must be closed with no crossing lines.
7. [4] — 1 mark each. Shapes must look regular (all sides and angles visibly equal):
(a) Equilateral triangle   (b) Square   (c) Regular pentagon   (d) Regular hexagon.
8. [12] — 2 marks each (1 for a valid drawing, 1 for showing the defining properties clearly):
(a) Square: all four sides equal, all angles 90°.
(b) Rectangle: two pairs of equal sides, all angles 90°; must not be a square.
(c) Rhombus: all four sides equal, opposite angles equal; must not look like a square.
(d) Parallelogram: two pairs of parallel sides; must not look like a rectangle.
(e) Kite: two pairs of adjacent equal sides; one axis of symmetry.
(f) Trapezium: exactly one pair of parallel sides.
9. [6] — 2 marks each:
(a) Quadrilateral with two right angles (marked), one acute angle and one obtuse angle, all four labelled. Angles must visibly sum to 360°. [1 mark for valid quadrilateral with two right angles; 1 mark for correct acute/obtuse pair.]
(b) Pentagon with three right angles marked; the other two angles must each be greater than 90° (they sum to 270°, so each is 135° if equal). [1 mark for pentagon with three right angles; 1 mark for remaining angles plausibly summing to 270°.]
(c) Octagon with at least four right angles, forming a non-convex (staircase-style) shape. [1 mark for an 8-sided closed shape; 1 mark for at least four visible right angles.]
10. [6] — 2 marks each:
(a) Two equilateral triangles joined along one side forming a rhombus (accept "diamond"). [1 mark for correct shape; 1 mark for correct name.]
(b) A square with one equilateral triangle on top and one on the bottom, forming a 6-sided shape (hexagon). Triangles must share a full side with the square. [1 mark for hexagon shape; 1 mark for correct construction.]
(c) A creative pattern using at least 3 regular polygons. [1 mark for using 3 or more regular polygons; 1 mark for a coherent, connected pattern.]

Angle: A measure of rotation between two lines that meet at a point.
Polygon: A closed 2D shape made from straight lines only (sides do NOT have to be equal length). The lines must not cross each other.
Regular Polygon: A special polygon where ALL sides are equal length AND ALL angles are equal.
Quadrilateral: Any polygon with exactly 4 sides.

Section A: Drawing Basic Angles

1 Draw the following angles in the boxes provided [3]

Instructions: Use your protractor to draw each angle accurately. Label each angle clearly.

a) An acute angle

(Any angle less than 90°)

b) An obtuse angle

(Any angle between 90° and 180°)

c) An angle of 56°

(Use your protractor!)

2 Draw these specific angles using your protractor [4]

a) 35°

b) 125°

c) 90° (right angle)

d) 160°

Section B: Drawing Combinations of Lines and Angles

3 Draw the following combinations of lines and angles [5]

a) Draw three lines that meet at a point, forming two acute angles

Hint: Start with a point, then draw three lines from it. Check that two of the angles formed are acute (less than 90°).

b) Draw four lines that meet at a point, with one right angle and two obtuse angles

Hint: Use your protractor to ensure accuracy.

c) Draw two intersecting lines forming angles of 45° and 135°

Hint: When two straight lines cross, they create two pairs of equal angles.

Section C: Types of Triangles

4 Draw these triangles based on the given descriptions [5]

Tip: Try drawing more than one example of each triangle type in the box to show different variations!

a) An equilateral triangle

All sides equal, all angles 60°

b) An isosceles triangle

Two sides equal, two angles equal

c) A right-angled triangle

One angle = 90°

d) A scalene triangle

All sides different lengths

e) A right-angled isosceles triangle

One 90° angle, two equal sides

Section D: Understanding and Drawing Polygons

What is a Polygon?
A polygon is a closed 2D shape made entirely from straight lines. The lines must connect to form a complete shape with no gaps. The lines must NOT cross each other. The sides do NOT have to be the same length (unless it's a regular polygon).
5 Which of these are polygons? Write YES or NO [5]

a) A triangle ___________

b) A circle ___________

c) A square ___________

d) A shape with one curved side and three straight sides ___________

e) A pentagon (5-sided shape) ___________

6 Draw these polygons in the boxes [6]

Remember: Polygons are closed shapes made only from straight lines. The sides don't have to be the same length. Use a ruler!

a) A triangle (3 sides)

b) A quadrilateral (4 sides)

c) A pentagon (5 sides)

d) A hexagon (6 sides)

e) A heptagon (7 sides)

f) An octagon (8 sides)

Section E: Regular Polygons

Regular Polygons:
A regular polygon has ALL sides equal in length AND ALL angles equal in size.
Examples: equilateral triangle, square, regular pentagon, regular hexagon
7 Draw these regular polygons as accurately as you can [4]

a) An equilateral triangle

(All sides equal, all angles 60°)

b) A square

(All sides equal, all angles 90°)

c) A regular pentagon

(5 equal sides, 5 equal angles)

d) A regular hexagon

(6 equal sides, 6 equal angles)

Section F: Special Quadrilaterals

8 Draw a few examples of each special quadrilateral [12]

Use a ruler and pay attention to the specific properties of each shape!

a) Squares

All sides equal, all angles 90°

b) Rectangles (not squares)

Opposite sides equal, all angles 90°

c) Rhombuses

All sides equal, opposite angles equal

d) Parallelograms (not rectangles)

Opposite sides parallel and equal

e) Kites

Two pairs of adjacent equal sides

f) Trapeziums

One pair of parallel sides

Section G: Combining Polygons and Angles

9 Draw shapes with specific angle requirements [6]

a) Draw a quadrilateral with two right angles, one acute angle and one obtuse angle

Hint: Angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Two right angles account for 180°, so the remaining two angles must also sum to 180° — meaning one must be acute and one obtuse. Label all four angles clearly.

b) Draw a pentagon where three angles are 90° and mark them

Hint: Angles in a pentagon sum to 540°. Three right angles account for 270°, leaving 270° shared between the other two angles. Try drawing a staircase-style or L-shaped pentagon. Use the right angle symbol to mark the 90° angles.

c) Draw an octagon with at least four right angles

Hint: An octagon has 8 sides. Try drawing a staircase or cross-like shape — these naturally produce right angles. Your octagon will be non-convex (some corners will point inward).

10 Create composite shapes (combining polygons) [6]

a) Draw a shape made by joining two equilateral triangles together along one side

What is this shape called?

Name: _______________________________________________

b) Draw a hexagon by combining a square and two equilateral triangles

Place one triangle on top of the square and one on the bottom.

c) Draw a pattern using at least 3 regular polygons of your choice

Be creative! The polygons can be the same or different types.

Total: 56 marks

Mark Scheme

1. [3] — 1 mark each for:
(a) Any angle clearly less than 90°, labelled as acute.
(b) Any angle clearly between 90° and 180°, labelled as obtuse.
(c) An angle of 56° ± 2°, drawn with a protractor and labelled.
2. [4] — 1 mark each for angles within ± 2°:
(a) 35°   (b) 125°   (c) 90° (right angle symbol acceptable)   (d) 160°
3. [5]
(a) [2] Three rays from a common point; two of the three gaps between rays are acute (less than 90°). The third gap will be a reflex angle. Award 1 mark for three rays meeting at a point, 1 mark for two visible acute angles.
(b) [2] Four rays from a common point; one gap is 90° (± 2°), and at least two other gaps are obtuse. Award 1 mark for correct structure, 1 mark for correct angle types.
(c) [1] Two straight lines crossing; all four angles labelled as 45°, 135°, 45°, 135° (or angles showing two pairs of equal vertically opposite angles).
4. [5] — 1 mark each for a correctly drawn and labelled example:
(a) Equilateral triangle: all three sides equal length, all angles 60°.
(b) Isosceles triangle: exactly two sides equal, base angles equal.
(c) Right-angled triangle: one angle of 90° (right angle symbol required).
(d) Scalene triangle: all three sides visibly different lengths.
(e) Right-angled isosceles triangle: one 90° angle and two 45° angles; two equal sides.
5. [5] — 1 mark each:
(a) YES   (b) NO (circle has a curved side)   (c) YES   (d) NO (has a curved side)   (e) YES
6. [6] — 1 mark each for a closed shape with straight lines only and the correct number of sides:
(a) 3 sides   (b) 4 sides   (c) 5 sides   (d) 6 sides   (e) 7 sides   (f) 8 sides.
Sides do not need to be equal. Shape must be closed with no crossing lines.
7. [4] — 1 mark each. Shapes must look regular (all sides and angles visibly equal):
(a) Equilateral triangle   (b) Square   (c) Regular pentagon   (d) Regular hexagon.
8. [12] — 2 marks each (1 for a valid drawing, 1 for showing the defining properties clearly):
(a) Square: all four sides equal, all angles 90°.
(b) Rectangle: two pairs of equal sides, all angles 90°; must not be a square.
(c) Rhombus: all four sides equal, opposite angles equal; must not look like a square.
(d) Parallelogram: two pairs of parallel sides; must not look like a rectangle.
(e) Kite: two pairs of adjacent equal sides; one axis of symmetry.
(f) Trapezium: exactly one pair of parallel sides.
9. [6] — 2 marks each:
(a) Quadrilateral with two right angles (marked), one acute angle and one obtuse angle, all four labelled. Angles must visibly sum to 360°. [1 mark for valid quadrilateral with two right angles; 1 mark for correct acute/obtuse pair.]
(b) Pentagon with three right angles marked; the other two angles must each be greater than 90° (they sum to 270°, so each is 135° if equal). [1 mark for pentagon with three right angles; 1 mark for remaining angles plausibly summing to 270°.]
(c) Octagon with at least four right angles, forming a non-convex (staircase-style) shape. [1 mark for an 8-sided closed shape; 1 mark for at least four visible right angles.]
10. [6] — 2 marks each:
(a) Two equilateral triangles joined along one side forming a rhombus (accept "diamond"). [1 mark for correct shape; 1 mark for correct name.]
(b) A square with one equilateral triangle on top and one on the bottom, forming a 6-sided shape (hexagon). Triangles must share a full side with the square. [1 mark for hexagon shape; 1 mark for correct construction.]
(c) A creative pattern using at least 3 regular polygons. [1 mark for using 3 or more regular polygons; 1 mark for a coherent, connected pattern.]

sheets.oldHtml:
Geometry and Shapes

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
4.1 Angles & Polygons
4.2 Circles
Key Concepts: Angles in polygons, circle theorems, area and perimeter calculations. Sum of interior angles in an n-sided polygon = (n-2) × 180°. Circle area = πr², circumference = 2πr.

Section A: Angles and Polygons

1. Calculate the sum of interior angles in: [3]
(a) A pentagon
(b) An octagon
(c) A decagon
2. A regular hexagon has 6 equal interior angles. [3]
(a) Calculate each interior angle
(b) Calculate each exterior angle

Section B: Circle Properties

3. A circle has radius 7 cm. [3]
(a) Calculate the circumference (use π = 22/7)
(b) Calculate the area
4. A circular garden has diameter 14 m. [2]
(a) Calculate the area of the garden
(b) If fencing costs £12 per meter, calculate the cost to fence the perimeter

Section C: Composite Shapes

5. A shape consists of a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm with a semicircle on one 5 cm side. [3]
(a) Calculate the total area
(b) Calculate the total perimeter
Total marks: 14

Mark Scheme

1. (a) (5-2) × 180° = 540° [1]
(b) (8-2) × 180° = 1080° [1]
(c) (10-2) × 180° = 1440° [1]
2. (a) Sum = (6-2) × 180° = 720°; Each angle = 720°/6 = 120° [2]
(b) Exterior angle = 180° - 120° = 60° (or 360°/6) [1]
3. (a) C = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 cm [2]
(b) A = πr² = (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm² [1]
4. (a) r = 7 m; A = π × 49 = 154 m² [1]
(b) C = 44 m; Cost = 44 × 12 = £528 [1]
5. (a) Rectangle area = 40 cm²; Semicircle area = π(2.5)²/2 = 9.82 cm²; Total ≈ 49.82 cm² [2]
(b) Perimeter = 8 + 8 + 5 + semicircle arc = 21 + π(2.5) ≈ 28.85 cm [1]

sheets.oldHtml:
Trigonometry

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
4.1 Trigonometric Ratios
4.2 Sine & Cosine Rules
4.3 Application
Key Concepts: Trigonometry involves the relationships between angles and sides in triangles. The main ratios are sine, cosine, and tangent (SOH CAH TOA). The sine and cosine rules allow you to find missing sides and angles in non-right triangles.
Hypotenuse Adjacent Opposite θ sin θ = Opposite/Hypotenuse cos θ = Adjacent/Hypotenuse tan θ = Opposite/Adjacent

Section A: Basic Trigonometric Ratios

1. For a right-angled triangle with angle θ, the opposite side is 5 cm and the hypotenuse is 13 cm. [2]
(a) Calculate sin θ
(b) Calculate cos θ
2. A ladder leans against a wall at an angle of 65° to the ground. The ladder is 4 m long. [2]
(a) How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
(b) How far from the wall is the base of the ladder?
3. In a right-angled triangle, tan θ = 3/4. [2]
(a) Find sin θ (assuming θ is acute)
(b) Find cos θ

Section B: Sine and Cosine Rules

4. In triangle ABC: AB = 8 cm, BC = 10 cm, and angle ABC = 60°. [3]
Use the cosine rule to find AC.
5. In triangle PQR: PQ = 7 cm, QR = 9 cm, PR = 11 cm. [3]
Use the cosine rule to find angle PQR to the nearest degree.
6. In triangle XYZ: angle X = 45°, angle Y = 60°, XY = 10 cm. [3]
Use the sine rule to find YZ.

Section C: Applications and Problem Solving

7. From a point on level ground, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is 35°. After walking 50 m closer to the building, the angle of elevation becomes 50°. [4]
Calculate the height of the building.
8. Two ships leave a port at the same time. Ship A travels on a bearing of 040° at 20 km/h. Ship B travels on a bearing of 100° at 15 km/h. Calculate the distance between the ships after 2 hours. [4]
Total marks: 24

Mark Scheme

1. (a) sin θ = 5/13 = 0.385 [1]
(b) cos θ = 12/13 = 0.923 [1]
2. (a) Height = 4 × sin(65°) = 3.63 m [1]
(b) Distance = 4 × cos(65°) = 1.69 m [1]
3. If tan θ = 3/4, then opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = 5 [1]
(a) sin θ = 3/5 = 0.6
(b) cos θ = 4/5 = 0.8 [1]
4. AC² = 8² + 10² - 2(8)(10)cos(60°) = 64 + 100 - 80 = 84 [2]
AC = 9.17 cm [1]
5. cos(Q) = (49 + 81 - 121)/(2 × 7 × 9) = 9/126 [2]
angle Q = 85.7° ≈ 86° [1]
6. Angle Z = 180° - 45° - 60° = 75° [1]
YZ/sin(45°) = 10/sin(75°) [1]
YZ = 10 × sin(45°)/sin(75°) = 7.32 cm [1]
7. Using two equations with tan: h/d = tan(35°) and h/(d-50) = tan(50°) [2]
Solving: d = 92.9 m, h = 65.1 m [2]
8. Distance travelled by A = 40 km, by B = 30 km [1]
Angle between directions = 100° - 40° = 60° [1]
Using cosine rule: d² = 40² + 30² - 2(40)(30)cos(60°) = 1600 + 900 - 1200 = 1300 [1]
d = 36.06 km [1]

Vectors and Transformations

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
5.1 Vectors
5.2 Transformations
Key Concepts: Vectors represent magnitude and direction. Column vectors show horizontal and vertical components. Transformations include translations, reflections, rotations, and enlargements.

Section A: Vector Operations

1. Given vectors a = (3, 2) and b = (1, 4): [3]
(a) Find a + b
(b) Find 2a
(c) Find a - b
2. Calculate the magnitude of vector v = (5, 12) [2]

3. Describe the transformation that maps: [3]

(b) Point (4, 1) to (-4, 1)
(c) Point (3, 2) to (6, 4)

(c) Enlargement scale factor 2, center origin [1]
4. (a) A'(-1, 1), B'(-3, 1), C'(-2, 3) [2]

sheets.spec: 6.1 Data & Sampling6.2 Averages & Spread6.3 Probability & Distributions
sheets.oldHtml:
Statistics and Probability

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
6.1 Data & Sampling
6.2 Averages & Spread
6.3 Probability & Distributions
Key Concepts: Statistics involves collecting, analyzing, and interpreting data. Measures of central tendency include mean, median, and mode. Measures of spread include range and standard deviation. Probability is the likelihood of an event occurring, ranging from 0 to 1.

Section A: Data Analysis and Averages

1. The test scores of 10 students are: 45, 52, 61, 58, 71, 48, 65, 59, 74, 66. [3]
(a) Calculate the mean
(b) Find the median and mode
(c) Calculate the range
2. The frequency table below shows heights of 20 students. [3]
Height (cm) 150-159 160-169 170-179 180-189
Frequency 3 8 7 2
Calculate the estimated mean height.
3. Two datasets have the same mean of 50, but Dataset A has a range of 10 and Dataset B has a range of 50. [2]
Which dataset is more dispersed? Explain your answer.

Section B: Probability

4. A bag contains 5 red balls, 3 blue balls, and 2 green balls. A ball is drawn at random. [3]
(a) What is the probability of drawing a red ball?
(b) What is the probability of drawing a ball that is not blue?
(c) If a red ball is drawn and not replaced, what is the probability that the second ball is also red?
5. A fair coin is flipped 3 times. [3]
(a) List all possible outcomes
(b) What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
(c) What is the probability of getting at least one tail?
6. Two events A and B are independent. P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. [2]
(a) Find P(A and B)
(b) Find P(A or B)

Section C: Problem Solving

7. In a class of 30 students, 18 study French and 15 study Spanish. 8 students study both languages. [3]
(a) How many students study only French?
(b) How many students study neither language?
(c) If a student is randomly selected, what is the probability they study Spanish?
8. A survey of 100 customers found that 60% prefer product A, 30% prefer product B, and 10% have no preference. If 20 more customers are surveyed and show the same distribution, what will be the new total preferring product A? [2]
Total marks: 24

Mark Scheme

1. (a) Mean = 599/10 = 59.9 [1]
(b) Median = (59 + 61)/2 = 60; No mode (or bimodal) [1]
(c) Range = 74 - 45 = 29 [1]
2. Estimated mean = (3×154.5 + 8×164.5 + 7×174.5 + 2×184.5)/20 [1]
= (463.5 + 1316 + 1221.5 + 369)/20 = 3370/20 = 168.5 cm [2]
3. Dataset B is more dispersed because it has a larger range [1]
The range is a measure of spread/dispersion [1]
4. (a) P(red) = 5/10 = 0.5 or 1/2 [1]
(b) P(not blue) = (5+2)/10 = 7/10 = 0.7 [1]
(c) P(second red | first red drawn) = 4/9 [1]
5. (a) HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT [1]
(b) P(exactly 2 heads) = 3/8 [1]
(c) P(at least 1 tail) = 7/8 [1]
6. (a) P(A and B) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12 [1]
(b) P(A or B) = 0.3 + 0.4 - 0.12 = 0.58 [1]
7. (a) Only French = 18 - 8 = 10 [1]
(b) Neither = 30 - (18 + 15 - 8) = 30 - 25 = 5 [1]
(c) P(Spanish) = 15/30 = 0.5 [1]
8. Total customers = 120; preferring A = 0.6 × 120 = 72 [2]

Statistics and Probability - Advanced

IGCSE Edexcel Mathematics
6.2 Statistical Analysis
6.3 Probability Theory
Key Concepts: Measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode). Standard deviation measures spread. Probability of independent and dependent events. Conditional probability uses P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B).

Section A: Measures of Spread

1. The dataset is: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 [4]
(a) Calculate the mean
(b) Calculate the range
(c) Calculate the standard deviation
2. Two datasets have the same mean but different standard deviations. Interpret this difference. [2]

Section B: Probability Calculations

3. A bag contains 3 red, 4 blue, and 5 green balls. [3]
(a) Find P(red)
(b) Find P(not green)
(c) Find P(red or blue)
4. Two dice are rolled. Find the probability of: [3]
(a) Sum = 7
(b) Both dice show the same number
(c) Sum > 10

Section C: Conditional Probability

5. Cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck. [3]
(a) Find P(2nd card is red | 1st card was red)
(b) Find P(both red)
Total marks: 20

Mark Scheme

1. (a) Mean = (3+5+7+9+11)/5 = 35/5 = 7 [1]
(b) Range = 11 - 3 = 8 [1]
(c) Variance = [(3-7)² + (5-7)² + (7-7)² + (9-7)² + (11-7)²]/5 = (16+4+0+4+16)/5 = 8; SD = √8 ≈ 2.83 [2]
2. Same mean indicates similar central value [1]; Different standard deviation means one dataset is more spread out/variable [1]
3. (a) P(red) = 3/12 = 1/4 [1]
(b) P(not green) = 7/12 [1]
(c) P(red or blue) = 7/12 [1]
4. (a) P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 [1]
(b) P(same) = 6/36 = 1/6 [1]
(c) P(sum > 10) = 3/36 = 1/12 [1]
5. (a) P(2nd red | 1st red) = 25/51 [2]
(b) P(both red) = (26/52) × (25/51) = 25/102 [1]

Mistake: wrong rearrangement. To find f you divide, not multiply.
f = v ÷ λ = 6 ÷ 3
f = 2 Hz
3. T = 20 ms
Mistake: ms was not converted to s.
20 ms = 0.02 s
f = 1 ÷ 0.02
f = 50 Hz

G  Challenge

1. Sonar
(a) The pulse goes down AND back up:
   distance = 2 × 600 = 1200 m
   v = d ÷ t = 1200 ÷ 0.8 = 1500 m/s
(b) f = 2.4 kHz = 2400 Hz
   λ = v ÷ f = 1500 ÷ 2400
(a) v = 1500 m/s   (b) λ = 0.625 m
Using 600 m gives 750 m/s, which is half the right answer. Always ask: does the wave go there and back?
2. Beach waves
(a) f = 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5 Hz
(b) T = 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 s
(c) λ = 4 m (crest to crest)
   v = f × λ = 0.5 × 4 = 2 m/s
(d) t = d ÷ v = 50 ÷ 2
(a) 0.5 Hz  (b) 2 s  (c) 2 m/s  (d) 25 s
The distance between two crests IS the wavelength.

1.4, 3.5–3.7 · wave speed, frequency, period, echoes and distance–speed–time
Name:
Reminder: data and equations
v = f × λ  ·  f = 1 / T  ·  speed = distance ÷ time
speed of light / EM waves, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
Worked step: 2.0 MHz = 2.0 × 10⁶ Hz; λ = v ÷ f (2 or 3 s.f.)
speed of sound in air = 340 m/s

A  Comparing waves

Wave A has twice the frequency of wave B and travels three times as fast. Wave B has a wavelength of 6.0 cm.
  1. Calculate the wavelength of wave A.
  2. Spot the mistake: a student says halving wave B's period (same speed) doubles its wavelength. Explain why that is wrong.
(a) λ =   (b)

B  Satellite TV

A geostationary satellite orbits 3.6 × 10⁴ km above the Earth's surface. It receives and sends TV signals at a frequency of 12 GHz.
  1. Calculate the wavelength of the signal in cm.
  2. Calculate the time taken for a signal to travel from a ground station up to the satellite and back down to a house.
  3. A news reporter talks to a studio through the satellite. Explain why there is a noticeable pause of about half a second before each reply.
(a) cm   (b) s

C  Oscilloscope trace

A microphone connected to an oscilloscope picks up a musical note. The trace is shown. The timebase is set to 2 ms per division.
  1. Calculate the time period of the sound wave.
  2. Calculate its frequency.
  3. Calculate its wavelength in air.
  4. The note is changed so its frequency doubles. How many divisions will one complete wave now take up?
(a) (b) (c) (d)
Side 1 of 2 · Turn over →

D  Approaching storm

During a storm, Sara counts 4.5 s between seeing a lightning flash and hearing the thunder.
  1. Calculate how far away the lightning is.
  2. Calculate how long the light takes to reach Sara, and explain why she can ignore it.
  3. Two minutes later the gap between flash and thunder is only 3.0 s. Calculate the average speed of the storm towards Sara.
(a) (b) (c)

E  Ultrasound scan

An ultrasound scanner sends pulses of frequency 2.0 MHz into the body. Ultrasound travels through soft tissue at 1540 m/s.
  1. Calculate the wavelength of the ultrasound in mm.
  2. An echo from the edge of an organ returns 65 μs after the pulse is sent. Calculate how deep the organ is, in cm.
  3. Each pulse lasts for 2.5 μs. Calculate how many complete waves are in one pulse, and the length of the pulse in mm.
(a) mm   (b) cm   (c) waves, mm

F  Locating an earthquake

An earthquake sends out two types of wave. P-waves travel at 8.0 km/s and S-waves at 4.5 km/s. A seismometer records the S-waves arriving 50 s after the P-waves.
  1. Calculate the distance from the seismometer to the earthquake, in km. Hint: call the distance d and write an expression for each travel time.
  2. The P-waves have a frequency of 2.0 Hz. Calculate their wavelength in km.

3b3 · Wave Speed: Multi-step Problems · Mark Scheme

IGCSE Edexcel Physics · KS4 · Double Award ★ Harder · Mark Scheme
Check each step of your working, not just the final number. Correct any mistakes in a different colour.
How to mark yourself: ✓ right value and unit  ·  follow-through counts: if an early answer is wrong but you used it correctly in a later part, credit the later working  ·  always check unit conversions first

A  Comparing waves

(a) λ = v ÷ f, so λA = (3v) ÷ (2f) = 1.5 × λB = 1.5 × 6.0 = 9.0 cm
(b) The wavelength halves. Because f = 1 ÷ T, halving T doubles f; v is unchanged, so λ = v ÷ f halves (to 3.0 cm).
(a) 9.0 cm  ·  (b) halves (3.0 cm)
Work with ratios rather than inventing numbers for v and f.

B  Satellite TV

(a) f = 12 GHz = 1.2 × 10¹⁰ Hz; λ = v ÷ f = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.2 × 10¹⁰ = 0.025 m = 2.5 cm
(b) 3.6 × 10⁴ km = 3.6 × 10⁷ m; distance up and back down = 2 × 3.6 × 10⁷ = 7.2 × 10⁷ m
    t = d ÷ v = 7.2 × 10⁷ ÷ 3.0 × 10⁸ = 0.24 s
(c) The question goes up and down (0.24 s), and the reply goes up and down again (0.24 s): about 0.48 s in total.
(a) 2.5 cm  ·  (b) 0.24 s  ·  (c) two return trips ≈ 0.48 s
km → m: multiply by 1000, so 3.6 × 10⁴ km = 3.6 × 10⁷ m.

C  Oscilloscope trace

(a) 2.5 waves fill 10 divisions, so 1 wave = 4 divisions; T = 4 × 2 ms = 8 ms = 0.008 s
(b) f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ 0.008 = 125 Hz
(c) λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 125 = 2.72 m (2.7 m to 2 s.f.)
(d) Frequency doubles, so time period halves: 4 ÷ 2 = 2 divisions.
(a) 0.008 s  ·  (b) 125 Hz  ·  (c) 2.7 m (2.72 m)  ·  (d) 2 divisions
Count divisions across several complete waves, then divide — more accurate than reading one wave by eye.

D  Approaching storm

(a) d = v × t = 340 × 4.5 = 1530 m
(b) t = 1530 ÷ 3.0 × 10⁸ = 5.1 × 10⁻⁶ s. This is tiny compared with 4.5 s (and human reaction time), so the light effectively arrives instantly.
(c) New distance = 340 × 3.0 = 1020 m; storm moved 1530 − 1020 = 510 m in 2 min (120 s)
    speed = 510 ÷ 120 = 4.25 m/s (4.3 m/s to 2 s.f.)
(a) 1530 m  ·  (b) 5.1 × 10⁻⁶ s  ·  (c) 4.3 m/s (4.25 m/s)
Convert 2 minutes to 120 s. Dividing by 2 gives 255 m/s — always sense-check whether a storm moves at jet speed!

E  Ultrasound scan

(a) f = 2.0 MHz = 2.0 × 10⁶ Hz; λ = v ÷ f = 1540 ÷ 2.0 × 10⁶ = 7.7 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.77 mm
(b) t = 65 μs = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ s; total distance = 1540 × 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.100 m (there and back)
    depth = 0.100 ÷ 2 = 0.050 m = 5.0 cm
(c) Number of waves = f × t = 2.0 × 10⁶ × 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 5 waves
    pulse length = 5 × 0.77 mm = 3.85 mm (3.9 mm to 2 s.f.)
(a) 0.77 mm  ·  (b) 5.0 cm  ·  (c) 5 waves, 3.9 mm (3.85 mm)
μ (micro) = × 10⁻⁶. Forgetting to halve an echo distance gives double the real depth (10 cm).

F  Locating an earthquake

(a) Time for S-waves − time for P-waves = 50 s:
    d ÷ 4.5 − d ÷ 8.0 = 50
    d × (0.2222 − 0.125) = 50 → d × 0.09722 = 50 → d = 50 ÷ 0.09722 = 514 km
(b) λ = v ÷ f = 8.0 ÷ 2.0 = 4.0 km
(a) 510 km (514 km)  ·  (b) 4.0 km
Keeping distance in km and speed in km/s cancels out the need to convert to metres here.
